paper.title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark
paper.code_data_availability: 'An Online Appendix for this article can be found at The Quarterly Journal of Economics online. …

registers.name_in_paper: the administrative wealth registry maintained by the Danish Statistical Agency
variables_mentioned: taxable wealth (total net wealth of households excluding pension wealth)

registers.name_in_paper: other administrative registries containing data on income and socioeconomic characteristics
registers.role: controls / descriptive statistics / tax ceiling status

registers.name_in_paper: land and real estate registries (used to record nonfinancial assets)

linkages: Individuals aggregated to households; wealth of married couples is household wealth, and individual-specific variables (age, schooling) are averaged across spouses
For the wealth-inequality series, household wealth of married couples is split equally between the spouses
The wealth registry is combined with administrative registries on income and socioeconomic characteristics
Parents cannot be linked to children born before 1960 in the Danish data, which rules out heterogeneity analysis by children

sample.universe: The entire Danish population with annual wealth data since 1980 (18,965,710 household-year observations in the full population pooled over 1982–88, Table I column (1))
sample.unit_of_observation: household-year (adults aged 20 or above); the life cycle profiles use individual-year observations
selection_rules: Focus on the 1989 reform rather than the 1997 abolition, because of the 1997 break in the taxable wealth series
Balanced panel of households observed in all years 1980-96
Assignment to treatment and control groups based on prereform variables, restricting attention to households whose status stays constant during 1982-88
Households that switch status during the treatment window (1982-88 in the baseline) are dropped from the estimation sample
Couples DD: couples and singles located within the exempted wealth range (97.6th-99.3rd percentiles), or couples below that range but within the top 5%

Ceiling DD: households within the top 1% of the wealth distribution, comparing unbound to bound taxpayers, dropping those only marginally bound (wealth tax liability would have to fall by at least 20% for them to become unbound)
Life cycle profiles: individuals in the top p% for at least three years of their observed life span, kept for their entire observed life span
sample.period: 1980-1996 for the quasi-experimental analysis; 1980-2012 for the wealth distribution and life cycle profiles
sample.n_observations: 104,839 (couples versus singles); 182,835 (couples within versus below); 94,503 (ceiling DD)
sample.n_individuals: Prereform group sizes (Table I, p. 349): 32,354 couples within (treatment); 10,815 singles within (control); 42,924 couples below (control); 35,966 unbound (treatment); 2,947 bound (control)

construction_notes: Taxable wealth equals total net wealth of households excluding pension wealth: cash, deposits, bonds, equities, housing, large durables and business assets, net of debts
For the behavioral analysis the paper uses reported taxable wealth (excluding pensions); imputations are used only for the wealth-distribution section

For the distribution section, funded pension wealth is imputed over 1980-2012 from individual-level pension wealth observed from 2012, allocating workers' pension wealth proportionally to wage incomes winsorized at the 99th percentile and retirees' proportionally to pension benefits
For the distribution section, noncorporate business assets are imputed by capitalizing business income and unlisted equities by capitalizing dividend income
Log wealth series in the event studies are normalized to 0 in the prereform year 1988
Life cycle profiles use normalized log wealth omega_iat = log(W_iat) - E[log(W_iat) | t]
Monetary values in Table I are reported in Danish Kroner in 2017 terms (the $/DKK exchange rate was 6.2 as of December 31, 2017)
Mechanical tax savings are computed assuming an annual rate of return of 5%, with counterfactual wealth imputed as 1988 wealth grown at the control group's growth rate
Elasticities are computed from equation (3), scaling the ITT effect by the expected log change in the net-of-tax rate; the elasticity with respect to (1 - tau)R - 1 assumes R = 1.05

claims.statement: ITT effects on log wealth: Average effect — Couples DD, couples versus singles within the exempted range, column (1) of Table II (no pretrend adjustment): exposure to the 1989 wealth tax cut raised log taxable wealth

treatment.label: Being a married couple whose prereform (1982–88) household taxable wealth lay in the range exempted by the 1989 reform (Treat_it)

register_source.value: Danish administrative wealth registry maintained by the Danish Statistical Agency (taxable wealth and marital/ceiling status); no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Treatment = married couples located between the 97.6th and 99.3rd percentiles of the household wealth distribution, whose wealth tax rate was cut to 0 by the doubling of the couples' exemption threshold between 1989 and 1992. Control = singles in the same household-wealth range, whose rate was cut from 2.2% to 1%. Status assigned from prereform variables and required constant over 1982–88.

timing.value: Treatment status assigned from prereform variables, required constant over 1982–88; the reform took effect on 1 January 1989 and the threshold change for couples was phased in 1989–92

outcome.label: log taxable wealth (log W_it)

register_source.value: Danish administrative wealth registry maintained by the Danish Statistical Agency (reported taxable wealth); no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Reported taxable wealth of the household: total net wealth excluding pension wealth, comprising cash, deposits, bonds, equities, housing, large durables and business assets net of debts, measured end-of-year in the Danish administrative wealth registry and entered in logs (log W_it). Series normalized to 0 in the prereform year 1988.

timing.value: average effect over the postreform window 1989–96 (years 1 to 8 after the reform)

estimand.target_population: Moderately wealthy Danish households (between roughly the 98th and 99th percentiles of the wealth distribution) treated by the 1989 exemption-threshold doubling for couples
estimand.time_horizon: average effect over the postreform window 1989–96 (years 1 to 8 after the reform)

population.description: Balanced panel of Danish households observed in all years 1980–96: married couples whose prereform household taxable wealth lay in the exempted range (97.6th–99.3rd percentiles, treatment) and singles in the same household-wealth range (control).
population.ages: Households of adults aged 20 or above; mean age in the comparison groups is between 57.8 and 63.6 years (Table I, p. 349)
population.period: 1980–1996 (prereform 1982–88 used for group assignment; postreform window 1989–96)
subgroups_defined: couples within the exempted wealth range (treatment)
singles within the exempted wealth range (control)
couples below the exempted wealth range, within the top 5% (control)
households unbound by the horizontal tax ceiling, top 1% (treatment)
households bound by the horizontal tax ceiling (control)
below/above median age (Online Appendix Tables A.I–A.II)
population.selection: Balanced panel of households observed in all years 1980–96; treatment and control status assigned from prereform variables with status required constant during 1982–88 and switchers dropped; the ceiling DD additionally conditions on being in the top 1% and drops households only marginally bound by the ceiling.

identification.source_of_variation: The 1989 Danish wealth tax reform: the marginal wealth tax rate was cut from 2.2% to 1% between 1989 and 1991 and the exemption threshold for married couples was doubled relative to singles between 1989 and 1992.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the 1989 reform, log taxable wealth in the treatment and control groups would have followed the same path.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inspection of prereform trends in Figures IV and VI; placebo reforms assumed in 1983–86 (Online Appendix Figures A.VI and A.XVI); robustness to the length of the prereform treatment window.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: wealth accumulation before 1989 was not affected by the reform, which was proposed on 3 November 1988, passed on 21 December 1988 and took effect on 1 January 1989.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The legislative timetable reported in footnote 16 (p. 344).

implies_edges.to: log taxable wealth in prereform years 1980-88

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is a balanced panel of households observed in all years 1980–96 whose treatment status (marital status and wealth bracket, or ceiling status) stays constant during 1982–88; switchers are dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the text (p. 346, footnote 19) and in the note to Table II.

implies_edges.to: sample inclusion (constant treatment status 1982-88, balanced panel 1980-96)

threats_discussed: Endogeneity of concurrent treatment status to the outcome, addressed by instrumenting with prereform status
Nonparallel prereform trends, addressed by a linear group-specific pretrend adjustment (specification (2))
Confounding shocks with different effects on different parts of the wealth distribution (couples within versus below)
Lack of prereform balance between bound and unbound households in the ceiling DD
Treatment effects that appear to start slightly before the reform in some specifications
Taxable wealth responses include evasion and avoidance as well as real saving responses
Marriage responses to the removal of the marriage penalty (Online Appendix Figure A.XIII), evidence not conclusive
Migration responses not considered; partial-equilibrium estimates only
robustness_checks: Alternative prereform windows for assigning treatment status: 1980–88, 1982–88 (baseline), 1984–88, 1986–88 (Online Appendix Figures A.V and A.XV)
Placebo reforms assumed in 1983, 1984, 1985 and 1986 (Online Appendix Figures A.VI and A.XVI)
Alternative control group of singles below the exempted range (Online Appendix Figures A.X–A.XII)
Alternative cuts for which bound households are dropped as only marginally bound (ceiling DD)
With and without linear differential pretrend adjustment (columns (1), (3), (5) versus (2), (4), (6))
Heterogeneity by age below and above the median (Online Appendix Tables A.I–A.II)
Bunching analysis at the exemption threshold (Online Appendix Section A)
unresolved_confounders: Evasion and avoidance responses, which the authors say would be difficult to separate out

estimator.value: OLS two-way fixed effects DD event study, reduced form on the prereform-based instruments

estimation.specification: Equation (1) — event study with household and year fixed effects, 1988 omitted
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered at the household level

source_table.value: Table II, column (1), row 'ITT effects on log wealth: Average effect'

mediators_claimed: Mechanical effect: the tax cut raises the after-tax rate of return, which increases wealth even with fixed behaviour (about one-tenth of the couples DD effect and about one-fifth of the ceiling DD effect after eight years)
Behavioural saving response: substitution effect on consumption proportional to the EIS and substitution effect on bequests proportional to the bequest elasticity, plus a wealth effect
Evasion and avoidance responses, which taxable wealth also captures

heterogeneity.dimension: Position in the wealth distribution (moderately wealthy couples DD versus very wealthy ceiling DD)
heterogeneity.finding: The abstract reports larger effects on the very wealthy than on the moderately wealthy; the ceiling DD TOT 1996 effect is 0.312 (0.106) against 0.186 (0.029) in the couples versus singles DD.

heterogeneity.dimension: Age (below versus above the median age in each estimation sample)
heterogeneity.finding: Online Appendix Tables A.I–A.II report heterogeneity by age; the estimates themselves are not reproduced in the main text.

value.claimed_domain: The authors present the Danish wealth tax as a way to estimate a key parameter for assessing the efficiency implications of capital taxes more broadly, while limiting the result to households that are already wealthy, conditional on staying in Denmark, and in partial equilibrium.
boundary_conditions: Effects on those who are already wealthy, not the forward-looking aspiration effect on those who aspire to become wealthy
Conditional on staying in Denmark; migration responses are not considered
Partial equilibrium; general equilibrium effects on asset prices and wage rates are not captured
Taxable wealth, so real savings responses are not separated from evasion and avoidance responses

theory_referenced: Saez and Stantcheva (2018): the long-run elasticity of capital supply as a sufficient statistic for optimal capital taxation
Chamley-Judd (Chamley 1986; Judd 1985)
Atkinson and Stiglitz (1976)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Compared to this literature, we consider a larger natural experiment and we estimate behavioral responses at the very top of the wealth distribution.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Labor supply responses to wealth taxation, explored with the same couples DD and ceiling DD strategies but not reported (footnote 28, p. 365: 'our explorations of the data shows no evidence of labor supply responses')
Heterogeneity by the presence and number of children, which the authors say is not feasible because parents cannot be linked to children born before 1960
Top 0.01% wealth shares, referred to as 'not shown' (p. 341)

treatment.label: Permanent cut in the wealth tax rate τ (a cut in the wealth tax rate of 1 percentage point, corresponding to the differential tax cut between couples and singles in the exempted range)

definition.value: A permanent reduction in the wealth tax rate τ from the prereform level of 0.022, of the size corresponding to the differential tax cut in the matching quasi-experiment: a cut in the wealth tax rate of 1 percentage point, corresponding to the differential tax cut between couples and singles in the exempted range.

timing.value: From period 0 (age 61) onward, permanently, over a 30-year simulated life span ending at age 90

outcome.label: 30-year effect on log taxable wealth (total effect)

register_source.value: Danish administrative wealth registry (the empirical life cycle profile of taxable wealth and the quasi-experimental moments the model is calibrated to); no DST register code is given in the paper

definition.value: Simulated change in log taxable wealth 30 years after a permanent cut in the wealth tax rate, for a representative household followed from age 61 (t = 0) to age 90 (t = T). Includes both the mechanical and the behavioral component.

timing.value: 30 years after the tax cut (ages 61 to 90 of the simulated life span)

magnitude.interpretation: At the end of life, wealth is 30% higher than it would have been absent the reform.

estimand.target_population: A representative household in the wealth range matched by this experiment: the top 1% sample over ages 60–90, standing in for the moderately wealthy between the 98th and 99th percentile cutoffs
estimand.time_horizon: 30 years after the tax cut (ages 61 to 90 of the simulated life span)

population.description: Representative-agent simulation calibrated to the empirical life cycle profile of taxable wealth of individuals who reach the top 1% (couples DD) or the top 0.3% (ceiling DD) at some point in their lives, over ages 60–90 in 1980–2012, together with the eight annual TOT moments from the 1989 reform.
population.ages: Ages 61 (t = 0) to 90 (t = T) of the simulated life span; the empirical profiles are measured between ages 20 and 90
population.period: Quasi-experimental moments from 1989–96; empirical life cycle profiles from 1980–2012; the simulation runs over a 30-year life span
subgroups_defined: top 1% sample (moderately wealthy, couples DD)
top 0.3% sample (very wealthy, ceiling DD)
low return (R = 1.05) versus high return (R = 1.07)
population.selection: Individuals selected for being in the top p% for at least three years of their observed life span and kept in the data for their entire observed life span; wealth of married couples split equally between spouses.

identification.source_of_variation: The quasi-experimental TOT effects of the 1989 Danish wealth tax reform for 1989–96, combined with the empirical life cycle profile of taxable wealth at the top of the distribution, used to calibrate a life cycle model with utility of residual wealth and to simulate it forward.

key_assumptions.assumption: The life cycle model with warm-glow utility of residual wealth (equations (4)–(5)) describes the savings behaviour of wealthy, older Danish households; precautionary saving, uncertainty, labour supply and estate taxes are abstracted from.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the facts that most of the top 1% are above age 50 and that the wealthy keep accumulating wealth into old age (Figure VIII); labour supply assumed inelastic citing Kleven and Schultz (2014) and Kleven (2014).

key_assumptions.assumption: The gross rate of return R is time invariant and known, set to R = 1.05 in this column (low return); the discount factor δ and the bequest weight A are calibrated to match the observed wealth path between ages 60 and 90.
key_assumptions.supported_by: R = 1.05 justified as within the range of estimated returns at the top of the wealth distribution (Fagereng et al. 2016); R = 1.07 shown as a robustness column.

key_assumptions.assumption: The quasi-experimental TOT estimates for 1989–96 are unbiased moments of the model-implied effects, so that minimising the quadratic loss in equation (19) identifies σ and α; average wealth growth during the last 10 years of life is imposed to be unchanged by the reform.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eight annual TOT moments for two parameters, plus the observed flatness of the end-of-life wealth profile before and after the reform (Online Appendix Figure A.XVIII).

definition.value: The curvature parameter of the warm-glow utility of residual wealth V(W_{T+1}) in equation (5), which the paper calls a bequest elasticity; calibrated jointly with σ to match the eight annual TOT moments from the 1989 reform subject to the requirement that average wealth growth in the last 10 years of life is unchanged by the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: The life cycle model with warm-glow utility of residual wealth (equations (4)–(5)) describes the savings behaviour of wealthy, older Danish households; precautionary saving, uncertainty, labour supply and estate taxes are abstracted from.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the facts that most of the top 1% are above age 50 and that the wealthy keep accumulating wealth into old age (Figure VIII); labour supply assumed inelastic citing Kleven and Schultz (2014) and Kleven (2014).

key_assumptions.assumption: The gross rate of return R is time invariant and known, set to R = 1.07 in this column (high return); the discount factor δ and the bequest weight A are calibrated to match the observed wealth path between ages 60 and 90.
key_assumptions.supported_by: R = 1.05 justified as within the range of estimated returns at the top of the wealth distribution (Fagereng et al. 2016); R = 1.07 shown as a robustness column.

key_assumptions.assumption: The quasi-experimental TOT estimates for 1989–96 are unbiased moments of the model-implied effects, so that minimising the quadratic loss in equation (19) identifies σ and α; average wealth growth during the last 10 years of life is imposed to be unchanged by the reform.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eight annual TOT moments for two parameters, plus the observed flatness of the end-of-life wealth profile before and after the reform (Online Appendix Figure A.XVIII).
